questions.q: What is the defining characteristic of symmetric encryption, like AES?
options: No key is required at all
It can only encrypt text, never binary files
A different key is used for encryption and decryption, and neither is ever shared
One shared key is used to both encrypt and decrypt the data
questions.explain: Symmetric encryption uses a single shared key for both directions, which is also what makes it computationally fast.

questions.q: What is the 'key-exchange problem' that symmetric encryption faces?
options: There is no such problem with symmetric encryption
AES cannot be used on more than one device
Symmetric keys expire after exactly 24 hours
Both sides need the same secret key, but sending it in plain text over the network exposes it to anyone watching
questions.explain: Safely getting a shared secret key to both parties over a network that might already be observed is the core challenge symmetric encryption can't solve alone.

questions.q: In asymmetric encryption, what can safely be shared with anyone?
options: The private key
Both keys equally
The public key
Neither key is ever meant to be shared
questions.explain: The public key can be distributed openly; only the private key, which never leaves its owner, must stay secret.

questions.q: Why is asymmetric encryption (like RSA) not used to encrypt large volumes of bulk data on its own?
options: Asymmetric encryption cannot produce a decryptable ciphertext
The math involved is far more computationally expensive and slower than symmetric encryption
It is illegal to use asymmetric encryption on large files
It is actually faster than symmetric encryption and is always preferred
questions.explain: Asymmetric encryption's math is much more expensive than symmetric encryption, so it is reserved for small, critical exchanges like a session key.

questions.q: How does TLS (the protocol behind HTTPS) actually combine symmetric and asymmetric encryption?
options: It alternates randomly between the two for every single request
It uses only asymmetric encryption for the entire connection, start to finish
It uses asymmetric encryption during the handshake to exchange a symmetric session key, then uses that session key for the rest of the connection
It uses only symmetric encryption and never touches asymmetric encryption
questions.explain: Asymmetric encryption solves the key-exchange problem once at the start; the fast symmetric session key then handles all the actual traffic.
